content: The composition of influenza virus vaccines for the 2005 Southern Hemisphere influenza season, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), included the following strains: an A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like virus, an A/Wellington/1/2004 (H3N2)-like virus, and a B/Shanghai/361/2002-like virus. The B/Shanghai/361/2002 strain was represented by B/Shanghai/361/2002, B/Jilin/20/2003, and B/Jiangsu/10/2003 at the time. For the 2005–2006 Northern Hemisphere influenza season, the vaccines produced contained an A/New Caledonia/20/1999-like (H1N1) virus, an A/California/7/2004-like (H3N2) virus (or the antigenically equivalent strain A/New York/55/2004), and a B/Jiangsu/10/2003-like virus. During this season, influenza and pneumonia-related deaths in the U.S. were below those of a typical flu season. Of the influenza A viruses identified, 84% were influenza A, and the remainder were influenza B. Among patients with influenza A, 80% had viruses identical or similar to the A strains in the vaccine. However, 70% of individuals testing positive for influenza B had Type B Victoria lineage viruses, which were not included in the vaccine. Influenza A (H3N2) viruses predominated overall, but influenza B viruses became more frequently isolated later in the season. Influenza A (H1N1) viruses circulated at low levels throughout the season. Nationally, influenza activity was low from October through early January, increased in February, and peaked in early March. Although peak activity was less intense compared to the previous three seasons, elevated activity persisted for a longer duration, possibly due to regional differences in the timing and intensity of influenza B activity later in the season. For the 2006 Southern Hemisphere influenza season, the WHO recommended a vaccine composition that included an A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like virus, an A/California/7/2004 (H3N2)-like virus (with A/New York/55/2004 used at the time), and a B/Malaysia/2506/2004-like virus. The 2006–2007 Northern Hemisphere influenza vaccine composition, recommended by the WHO on February 15, 2006, and by the U.S. FDA’s Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (VRBPAC) on February 17, 2006, included an A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like virus, an A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2)-like virus (represented by A/Wisconsin/67/2005 and A/Hiroshima/52/2005 strains), and a B/Malaysia/2506/2004-like virus (from B/Malaysia/2506/2004 and B/Ohio/1/2005 strains of the B/Victoria/2/87 lineage). For the 2007 Southern Hemisphere influenza season, the WHO recommended a vaccine composition on September 20, 2006, that included an A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like virus, an A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2)-like virus (represented by A/Wisconsin/67/2005 and A/Hiroshima/52/2005 strains), and a B/Malaysia/2506/2004-like virus. The 2007–2008 Northern Hemisphere influenza vaccine composition, recommended by the WHO on February 14, 2007, included an A/Solomon Islands/3/2006 (H1N1)-like virus, an A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2)-like virus (represented by A/Wisconsin/67/2005 and A/Hiroshima/52/2005 strains), and a B/Malaysia/2506/2004-like virus. For the 2008 Southern Hemisphere influenza season, the WHO recommended a vaccine composition on September 17–19, 2007, that included an A/Solomon Islands/3/2006 (H1N1)-like virus, an A/Brisbane/10/2007 (H3N2)-like virus, and a B/Florida/4/2006-like virus. In veterinary medicine, influenza vaccination aims to achieve four goals: (i) protection from clinical disease, (ii) protection from infection with virulent virus, (iii) prevention of virus shedding, and (iv) serological differentiation of infected from vaccinated animals (the DIVA principle). However, no commercially available or experimentally tested influenza vaccines have been shown to meet all these criteria. In horses, equine influenza can cause fever, a dry hacking cough, nasal discharge, depression, and reluctance to eat or drink, with recovery typically occurring within 2–3 weeks. Vaccination schedules generally involve a primary course of two doses administered 3–6 weeks apart, followed by boosters at 6–12 month intervals. However, in high-risk situations, more frequent administration may be necessary to maintain protective antibody levels. Poultry vaccines for avian influenza are produced at low cost and are not filtered or purified to the same standards as human vaccines. They often contain whole virus rather than just hemagglutinin, as in most human flu vaccines. Purification to human standards is significantly more expensive than producing unpurified vaccines from eggs, and there is no market for such costly veterinary vaccines. Poultry vaccines are adjuvanted with mineral oil to induce a strong immune response, but this can cause inflammation and abscesses. Accidental self-injection by poultry vaccinators can result in painful swelling or even loss of digits. The effectiveness of poultry vaccines may be limited, as they are often only vaguely similar to circulating flu strains. For example, some contain an H5N2 strain isolated in Mexico years ago. While partial protection may be sufficient for poultry, human vaccines require a much closer match to circulating strains to be effective. Swine influenza virus (SIV) vaccines are widely used in the swine industry in Europe and North America. Most commercial swine flu vaccines include H1N1 and H3N2 SIV strains. However, the evolution of the virus has led to inconsistent responses to traditional vaccines. Standard commercial vaccines are effective when the virus strains match closely enough to provide significant cross-protection. In more challenging cases, custom (autogenous) vaccines are created from specific virus isolates.
